outcome: Not settled, but the exact value f(n) = 2n (the pigeonhole ceiling) has been established since 26 January 2024 for every n from 1 to 76 except n = 75, through a CP-SAT construction for all n ≤ 60 (Prellberg, arXiv 2602.07751, 8 Feb 2026) and through site, OEIS and mailing-list records for n = 61–64, 65–74 and 76 (Prellberg, Heule); f(n) is still unknown for every n ≥ 75 beyond the listed cases, the asymptotic question (whether f(n) < 2n eventually, with growth constant conjectured as π/√3 ≈ 1.814) is unchanged as a conjecture, and a June 2026 MCTS paper reports empirical configurations of about 1.8n for 82 ≤ n ≤ 119.
problem_asks: The statement asks for f(n), the largest number of points that can be placed in the n × n grid so that no three are collinear, with lines of every slope counting. Unpacked: (1) for each n ≥ 1, the exact value of f(n); (2) because the question asks 'how many' for every n, the behaviour of f(n) as n grows, meaning its order and constant. Context at the frozen revision, not part of the ask: f(n) ≤ 2n by pigeonhole; an Erdős/Roth-type construction gives about n; Hall, Jackson, Sudbery and Wild give (3/2 − o(1))n; the Guy–Kelly heuristic conjectures growth cn with c ≈ 1.814 (originally quoted as 1.874). The statement itself does not assert that f(n) = 2n for all n, nor that f(n) < 2n for large n; it asks for the value.

events.what_happened: Lower-bound construction credited to Erdős via Roth (1951): for prime p the points (i, i² mod p) have no three collinear, and using the largest prime p ≤ n gives n − o(n) points. Pre-window context. Known only from the Wikipedia summary; the 1951 paper was not opened.
events.delivers: Lower bound f(n) ≥ (1 − o(1))n. Fixes the order of growth up to a constant; does not touch the exact value or the 2n ceiling.
events.remains: Exact f(n) for every n; the constant in the linear growth (the best known is 3/2 since 1975); tightness of 2n for large n.
events.directly_checkable: The construction is explicit: for small primes it can be checked by hand (a parabola modulo p meets any line in at most two points).
events.direction: Lower bound, consistent with every conjecture in play. No object contradicts the problem.
events.object: Explicit set {(i, i² mod p)} for prime p, giving about p points on the p × p grid with no three collinear; the secondary source does not give the exact grid convention.

events.what_happened: Guy and Kelly, 'The no-three-in-line problem', Canadian Mathematical Bulletin 11 (1968) 527–531, as summarised by Wikipedia and MathWorld: 2n configurations for small n (2 ≤ n ≤ 10 per the Wikipedia summary), and a heuristic conjecture that for large n at most (c + ε)n points are possible, with c = (2π²/3)^(1/3) ≈ 1.874. The primary paper was not opened (search link only).
events.delivers: Exact values f(n) = 2n for 2 ≤ n ≤ 10 (per the Wikipedia summary). A heuristic conjecture of growth c ≈ 1.874, later corrected.
events.remains: All n ≥ 11; the asymptotic constant.
events.directly_checkable: Small-n configurations are checkable by hand.
events.doubts: The heuristic is the one later found to contain an error (see guy-2004-correction); the 1.874 constant is superseded as a conjecture.
events.direction: Small-n attainment of the 2n ceiling; a heuristic that growth falls below 2n for large n, consistent with the open question.

events.what_happened: Hall, Jackson, Sudbery and Wild (1975): modular-hyperbola constructions giving 3(n − 2)/2 points when n/2 is prime, and by patching (3/2 − o(1))n for general n. This is still the best known asymptotic lower bound: Epoch, Wikipedia and the June 2026 MCTS paper (Table 1) all give it as such. Primary paper not opened.
events.delivers: Lower bound f(n) ≥ (3/2 − o(1))n for all n. Below the 2n ceiling and so does not settle the question.
events.remains: The gap between 3/2 and 2 in the linear constant; exact values for large n.
events.directly_checkable: Explicit hyperbola constructions; any given n can be checked by computer.
events.direction: Lower bound below the 2n ceiling; consistent with the Guy–Kelly picture of growth below 2n.
events.object: Explicit modular-hyperbola point sets (for n/2 prime, 3(n − 2)/2 points), extended to general n by patching to (3/2 − o(1))n points.

events.what_happened: Flammenkamp, 'Progress in the no-three-in-line problem', Journal of Combinatorial Theory Series A 60 (1992) 305–311, and 'Part II', 81 (1998) 108–113. Computer-found 2n configurations for all n ≤ 46 and for n = 48, 50, 52 (per OEIS, Sillke and MathWorld summaries; the Gustavus page reports a single solution each for 48, 50, 52). Primary papers not opened.
events.delivers: Exact values f(n) = 2n for n ≤ 46 and n = 48, 50, 52. Settles those single cases only.
events.remains: f(n) for n = 47, 49, 51 and for all n ≥ 53 until later events.

checked_by.who: Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A (refereed journal)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for both parts
checked_by.what_they_did: Published Part I (1992) and Part II (1998) after peer review

events.directly_checkable: The configurations are in Flammenkamp's solution database (readme); each is checkable by a brute-force collinearity test.
events.direction: The 2n ceiling is attained for these n; consistent with the ceiling being sharp for small n.
events.object: Explicit 2n-point configurations on the n × n grid for each listed n, found by computer search; the search method was not checked.

events.what_happened: Guy's note of October 2004, as quoted in OEIS A000769 and MathWorld (the note itself was not opened), records that Gábor Ellmann found an error in the Guy–Kelly heuristic; corrected, the heuristic gives 3c² = π², so c = π/√3 ≈ 1.813799. Voutier (2026) explains the error in detail. Pre-window.
events.revisions: Explained in arXiv 2603.00215 (27 Feb 2026); reproduced in arXiv 2609.25133 (20 Sep 2026).
events.delivers: A corrected conjectured growth constant c = π/√3 ≈ 1.814 replacing ≈ 1.874. A heuristic conjecture, not a bound.
events.remains: Everything: the corrected constant is unproven.
events.doubts: Dating and attribution of Ellmann's error disagree: 'last March' in Guy's October 2004 note (as quoted, pointing to March 2004); March 2005 per Flammenkamp's page; 2004 in Voutier's abstract, with 'March 2024' in Voutier's v1 body. Existence of the error and the corrected constant are consistent across sources.
events.direction: Lowers the conjectured growth constant from about 1.874 to about 1.814; both stay below 2n and both are conjectures.

events.what_happened: Thomas Prellberg's computer searches add exact 2n configurations for n = 47 to 56. OEIS A272651 dates the entries a(47)–a(56) to 28 October 2025. Flammenkamp's log records n = 58 on 28 October 2025 (OEIS dates a(58) to 23 November 2025). The December 2025 preprint arXiv 2512.11469 cites 'T. Prellberg, private communication, 2025' for exact 2n solutions for all n ≤ 58.
events.delivers: Exact f(n) = 2n for n = 47 to 56 (the ceiling is attained). Each is a single-n settlement of the question as worded.
events.remains: f(n) for n ≥ 57 at this date; all asymptotic content.
events.directly_checkable: Configurations are in Flammenkamp's searchable database (the readme reports 431,008 entries as of 31 Aug 2026); each is checkable by a collinearity test. No preprint contains them.
events.doubts: The only public records are an OEIS extension line and Flammenkamp's log; the 2025 'private communication' is cited by a preprint in which Prellberg is a co-author. The method for these entries is not stated.
events.direction: Attains the 2n ceiling for these n; says nothing about large n.
events.object: Explicit 2n-point configurations on n × n grids for n = 47–56 (and 58 per the log); the construction method is not stated for these entries.

events.what_happened: OEIS A272651 dates a(57)–a(58) to 23 November 2025 (Prellberg). Flammenkamp's log has n = 57 'at the end of November 2025' and calls it the first 2n solution for an odd n; the same log lists odd n up to 45 as already known.

events.direction: Attains the 2n ceiling for these n.
events.object: Explicit 2n configurations for n = 57 and n = 58.

events.what_happened: arXiv 2512.11469 (Ramanathan, Prellberg, Lewis, Joshi, R. Dandekar, Rajat Dandekar, Panat; cs.AI and math.CO), 'Three methods, one problem: Classical and AI approaches to no-three-in-line', v1 12 Dec 2025, v2 22 Dec 2025. Compares Gurobi integer linear programming (provably optimal up to 19 × 19), PatternBoost transformer learning and PPO reinforcement learning. PatternBoost matches known optimal values up to 14 × 14 and reaches 29 points on 15 × 15 (optimum 30); PPO solves 10 × 10 and fails at 11 × 11. The ICML 2026 AI for Math workshop poster 'Four Methods, One Problem' (11 July 2026) adds a scientific-machine-learning gradient-flow method that finds optimal 2n configurations up to n = 18 in several cases.
events.revisions: v2 22 Dec 2025 (current on arXiv abs page); ICML 2026 workshop poster version 'Four Methods, One Problem' (listing read; poster body not read).
events.delivers: No new value of f(n). The AI and ILP results reproduce known optimal values 2n for n ≤ 14 (and ILP to 19); the 15 × 15 result (29 points) falls short of the known 30. The comparative claims are empirical and about methods.
events.remains: All of the question for n ≥ 20 (ILP stops at 19) and the asymptotics.

checked_by.who: ICML 2026 AI for Math Workshop programme (poster acceptance)
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted a poster version of the comparison; this is not a check of any mathematical claim

events.directly_checkable: The small optimal configurations (10 × 10, 14 × 14) are checkable by brute force; they are the known 2n values.
events.doubts: No new values are claimed; the 'first time' comparison claim is the authors' own; the poster is a workshop acceptance; the gradient-flow method's success is non-monotone per the poster abstract (n = 17 succeeded 0 of 10 times in one sweep, n = 18 succeeded 9 of 10).
events.direction: Neutral to the question: reproduces known 2n values and reports AI methods falling short beyond about 14 to 15.

systems.name: PatternBoost
systems.what_it_did: Transformer-based pattern learning applied to the no-three-in-line problem. Per the authors, it matches known optimal values up to 14 × 14, and the ICML version reports 29 points on 15 × 15 where the optimum is 30. The paper says it matches optima 'despite never observing optimal training examples'. No new values.
systems.basis_quote: We apply PatternBoost transformer learning and reinforcement learning (PPO) to this problem for the first time.

systems.name: PPO
systems.what_it_did: Proximal policy optimisation (reinforcement learning). Per the authors, it gives perfect solutions on 10 × 10 grids and fails at 11 × 11 because of constraint violations. No new values.
systems.basis_quote: PPO achieves perfect solutions on 10 by 10 grids but fails at 11 by 11 grids

ai.disclosed_cost: Not stated for the PatternBoost or PPO runs. The ICML 2026 listing says the gradient-flow method ran on Apple M2 hardware using Apple Metal.

events.what_happened: Thomas Prellberg, 'Constraint Satisfaction Programming for the No-three-in-line Problem', arXiv 2602.07751, submitted 8 Feb 2026 (one version as listed). Uses Google CP-SAT (version 9.12) with 90-degree rotational symmetry and gives explicit configurations with 2n points for every n ≤ 60; the paper says this moves the smallest n with f(n) = 2n unknown from 47 to 61. Section 1 also gives a probabilistic count, C(n, 2n), which the paper says becomes smaller than one once n ≥ 493, and states the conjecture D(n) < cn with c = π/√3 ≈ 1.81 from a probabilistic estimate. The paper says the Guy–Kelly heuristic 'exposes a clear weakness' and 'casts doubts as to its validity'. Code repository: github.com/ThomasPrellberg/no-three-in-line---CP-SAT (linked, not opened).
events.revisions: One version in the listing (v1, 8 Feb 2026). A search summary of its reference list gives 'forthcoming in J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 225 (2027)'; not verified.
events.delivers: Exact f(n) = 2n for all 1 ≤ n ≤ 60, by explicit configurations (the paper's Theorem 1: 'For 2 ≤ n ≤ 60 there exists a configuration'). Heuristic only: the probabilistic count drops below one at n ≥ 493, and the conjectured constant is π/√3. Neither heuristic is a theorem.
events.remains: f(n) for n ≥ 61 (the paper's own statement); the asymptotic constant; the heuristic is unproven.
events.directly_checkable: The 2n configurations for n ≤ 60 are explicit and checkable by a collinearity test; the paper's code is public at the repository linked above (not opened).
events.doubts: The heuristic part is heuristic, and the paper itself treats the Guy–Kelly heuristic as doubtful. The configurations come from the author's own CP-SAT runs; no independent reproduction is recorded. The v1 text the paper gives for its n = 61 and 62 attempts: 'no solution was found within 10^7 seconds'.
events.direction: Attains the ceiling 2n for all n ≤ 60. The heuristic part points toward f(n) < 2n for large n, in line with Guy–Kelly, but is not proved.
events.object: Explicit configurations of 2n points on the n × n grid with no three collinear, for every n ≤ 60, found by CP-SAT with 90-degree rotational symmetry. Each is checkable by a collinearity test.

events.what_happened: Paul M. Voutier, 'On the Guy-Kelly Conjecture for the No-Three-In-Line Problem', arXiv 2603.00215, v1 27 Feb 2026, v2 9 Mar 2026 (clarifications and credit to Prellberg added). Gives the details of Ellmann's error in the Guy–Kelly heuristic, which the abstract says had not appeared in the literature, and restates the corrected conjectured bound f_n ~ (π/√3)n. Credits Prellberg's arXiv 2602.07751 with a derivation of the corrected bound.
events.delivers: No value of f(n). A conjecture-level restatement of the corrected growth constant π/√3 ≈ 1.814; no bound.
events.remains: All of the question.
events.doubts: A short single-author note that proves nothing new. The derivation it cites is in Prellberg's 2602.07751 (Section 1, per the html). Kudriashov's September 2026 paper reproduces the constant by its own audit, but does not engage this note specifically.
events.direction: Restates a conjectured growth constant below 2n. Consistent with the Guy–Kelly picture; does not decide f(n).

events.what_happened: Prellberg's note 'Four-corner permutation tests for no-three-in-line configurations' on the Flammenkamp site, dated 27 June 2026. It argues that either of two conjectures about permutation-matrix quadrants on 2M × 2M no-three-in-line grids (the four-corner conjecture and the adjacent-permutation conjecture) implies Guy–Kelly Conjecture II (every configuration with horizontal and vertical mirror symmetry has the full symmetry of the square), given small-case checks for M ≤ 5.
events.delivers: A conditional implication between two unproven conjectures and Guy–Kelly Conjecture II. No value of f(n).
events.remains: All of f(n); Guy–Kelly II itself.
events.directly_checkable: The small cases are computational and checkable in principle; not inspected.
events.doubts: The four-corner conjecture is checked computationally only for N < 38, and the note says the adjacent-permutation conjecture has 'slightly less evidence'. The implication is conditional; the note does not prove Guy–Kelly II.
events.direction: Structural, about mirror-symmetric configurations; not about the maximum.

events.what_happened: Luoning Zhang, Xu Zhuang, Tianhao Wang and Nathan Kaplan, 'Geometry-Aware MCTS for Extremal Problems in Combinatorial Geometry', arXiv 2606.26399 (primary cs.AI; also cs.CG, cs.LG, math.CO), submitted 24 June 2026, one version. Proposes Monte Carlo tree search with incremental updates to the feasible action space. For the no-three-in-line problem (called Max-N3IL) it reports 'configurations of size roughly 1.8n for grids of size 82≤n≤119'; Table 1 lists this as '≈1.8n (Empirical Fit)' and compares it with Hall et al.'s (1.5 − ε)n. Table 4 (Appendix E) lists previous best-known values for n ≤ 80: 2n for n ≤ 70, and 140, 140, 140, 144, 148 for n = 72, 74, 76, 78, 80.
events.delivers: Lower bounds for the maximum at 82 ≤ n ≤ 119 of roughly 1.8n, described as an empirical fit. This lifts the known lower bound in that range above Hall et al.'s 1.5n. It does not give an exact value of f(n) for any n, and it is not an asymptotic bound. Nothing for n ≥ 120.
events.remains: Exact f(n) for 82 ≤ n ≤ 119; all n ≥ 120; the asymptotic constant; the n = 71–80 values are not from this paper.
events.directly_checkable: Configurations for each n in 82–119 are in the paper's figures or appendices; per-n sizes were not extracted. Validity is enforced by the search itself ('This ensures that any action taken preserves Φ'); no external checker is described.
events.doubts: The 1.8n figure is labelled an 'Empirical Fit' and the text gives no fit method, range or residuals. Per-n sizes were not extracted (Figure 6a plots |sT|/n for Max-N3IL). No independent check of the configurations is described. The paper's stated aim is 'new best-known computational results', not proofs.
events.direction: Lower bounds at 82–119 are consistent with the Guy–Kelly picture (c ≈ 1.81) and sit below the 2n ceiling. They do not show f(n) = 2n or f(n) < 2n for any n in that range.
events.object: Max-N3IL configurations (points on an n × n grid with no three collinear) of about 1.8n points for each n from 82 to 119, produced by the MCTS framework. Exact sizes per n were not extracted.

systems.name: Geometry-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework
systems.what_it_did: The authors' own search method, which produced the about-1.8n Max-N3IL configurations for 82 ≤ n ≤ 119. Uses UCT-style search, incremental feasibility updates and symmetry pruning. The implementation uses no learned model: Appendix A.2 says 'neural networks are not included in our current implementation'. The paper cites PPO and transformer baselines and FunSearch/AlphaEvolve only as prior work, not as tools it used.
systems.basis_quote: Notably, for Max-N3IL we find configurations of size roughly 1.8n for grids of size 82≤n≤119.

events.what_happened: Aleksei Kudriashov, 'Certified computations on no-three-in-line problems: exact values and witnesses in the cube, and the Guy-Kelly count in the plane', arXiv 2609.25133, single version listed 20 Sep 2026 (comments give 'v1.0 (21 Sep 2026)'), 27 pages. Four parts: (I) cube exact values a(1)–a(6) and certified bounds for n = 7–11 (three-dimensional, not this problem); (II) lower bounds for the no-four-coplanar problem, 9 ≤ n ≤ 29 (a different problem); (III) planar Guy–Kelly heuristic: audits the first-moment heuristic against exact counts up to n = 20 and derives a corrected constant, in closed form π/√3; reproduces the threshold crossing at n = 493; (IV) the direction spectrum of 2n-point solutions. Section 9 ('AI/tool-use disclosure') says the searches, programs and text were produced by autonomous AI agents (Anthropic Claude) under the author's direction. Certification: DRAT proofs checked by drat-trim for cube unsatisfiability results; each witness re-checked by a second program.
events.revisions: Comments list 'v1.0 (21 Sep 2026)'; listing shows one version.
events.delivers: Planar part only as a heuristic audit, not a theorem: the corrected Guy–Kelly constant π/√3 in closed form, and a heuristic threshold n = 493 at which the expected count of 2n configurations falls below one. The paper says whether the residual error is Θ(n) or Θ(n ln n) (which decides whether the constant survives) 'cannot be told by counting'. No value f(n) is settled and no new planar construction is claimed. The cube results concern the three-dimensional problem.
events.remains: Every planar value of f(n); a proof that the corrected constant holds.
events.directly_checkable: The cube witnesses and certificates are said to be in an ancillary archive on Zenodo (per the abstract; not opened).
events.doubts: Single author. Section 9 says that agents audited one another's work and that 'several errors reported in the repository were caught that way and not by their author', including an unverified symmetry pruning, so the process was error-prone before the checks. The paper concedes the key question for the planar constant is open. The Section 9 wording reached me through a summarising fetch and should be checked against the PDF.
events.direction: Heuristic: the Guy–Kelly first-moment count with corrected constant π/√3 ≈ 1.814 suggests that 2n configurations fail for large n (threshold 493), in line with the open conjecture that f(n) < 2n eventually. Not a proof and not a value.
events.object: None for the planar problem. The audit uses exact counts of 2n configurations for n ≤ 20 as data. Cube witnesses concern the three-dimensional problem.

disputes.summary: The date of Ellmann's error in the Guy–Kelly heuristic differs across sources: March 2004 (Guy's October 2004 note, as quoted), March 2005 (Flammenkamp's page), 2004 (Voutier's abstract) and March 2024 (Voutier's v1 body). This does not change the window status, since all are pre-window.
Heule's n = 76 solution is dated 10 August 2026 in Flammenkamp's log and 20 August 2026 in MathWorld's table.
OEIS EXTENSIONS dates conflict with the maintainer's log: n = 58 (28 Oct 2025 log; 23 Nov 2025 OEIS), n = 66 (9 Mar 2026 log; 20 Jun 2026 OEIS), n = 68 (23 Mar 2026 log; OEIS comment 20 Jun 2026).

The n = 61–64 results are credited to Prellberg by the maintainer's log and dated 20 Feb 2026 in OEIS. Voutier's v1 says the extension to n = 64 was reached by Prellberg in mid-February. The 8 Feb 2026 arXiv v1 stops at n = 60 and calls 61 the smallest unresolved case. No later preprint was located.

AI disclosure differs across the 2026 papers on this problem. Kudriashov (arXiv 2609.25133) says the searches, programs and text of the whole article were produced by autonomous AI agents (Anthropic Claude) under the author's direction. Prellberg (arXiv 2602.07751) says ChatGPT generated code implementing his models and helped with editorial checks. Ramanathan et al. (arXiv 2512.11469) name PatternBoost and PPO as methods but make no statement on how the paper was written. These are different kinds of disclosure, not a dispute about one result.

summary: Since 26 January 2024 the planar problem has moved in one specific way: the exact value f(n) = 2n, the pigeonhole ceiling, has been established for every n from 1 to 76 except n = 75. The ground for n ≤ 60 is an explicit CP-SAT construction in Prellberg's arXiv 2602.07751 (8 Feb 2026), which is the only preprint carrying the method. Values for n = 61–64 (Prellberg), 65, 67, 69, 70, 71, 72, 73, 76 (Heule), 66 and 68 (Prellberg) and 74 (Prellberg) rest on Flammenkamp's solution log, MathWorld's table, OEIS extension lines and a SeqFan post; I found no preprint, certificate or write-up for any of them, and the dates disagree across those records for n = 58, 66, 68 and 76. Each is a single-n settlement of the question as worded, so each counts as an event, but the frontier is maintained by one person's log. The asymptotic question is unchanged as a conjecture. The best proven lower bound is still Hall et al.'s (3/2 − o(1))n. The Guy–Kelly constant was corrected in 2004 to π/√3 ≈ 1.814; Voutier (27 Feb 2026) explains the error and proves nothing new; and two 2026 papers reproduce the constant as a heuristic: Prellberg's 2602.07751 gives a count C(n, 2n) that drops below one at n ≥ 493, and Kudriashov's 2609.25133 (20 Sep 2026) reproduces 493 and derives π/√3 by a self-described audit that concedes the key residual-error question is open. A June 2026 MCTS paper (2606.26399) reports Max-N3IL configurations of about 1.8n for 82 ≤ n ≤ 119 with the sizes labelled an 'Empirical Fit'. This lifts the known lower bound above Hall et al.'s 1.5n for that range, but it is not an exact value, not an asymptotic statement, and per-n sizes were not extracted. On AI: Ramanathan et al. (2512.11469, Dec 2025; ICML 2026 poster in July) apply PatternBoost and PPO, which reproduce known optima and produce no new f(n). Prellberg's 2602.07751 credits ChatGPT only with code and editorial help. Kudriashov's 2609.25133 is the strongest AI-in-result claim: its Section 9 says the searches, programs and text were produced by autonomous AI agents (Anthropic Claude) under the author's direction, and the planar Part III is inside that statement, though what it produces is a heuristic constant, not a value. The MCTS paper names its own Geometry-Aware MCTS framework and uses no learned model; whether that is an AI system is a judgement I leave open. Two 2026 AI credits are lead-only and are not in ai.systems because no authors' account was found: Flammenkamp's log credits Jacob Davies with 'the AI ChatGPT 5.6 Sol' for 619 plus 24 census solutions for already-settled n (24 and 30 July 2026), and credits Kudriashov with 'AI Claude from Anthropic' for 9 rot2 solutions (17 Aug 2026). No source credits an AI system with a new value of f(n). I found no Google, OpenAI or DeepMind result on this problem. Heule's runs are SAT, not AI. Epoch AI's open-problem page for this bullet asks for an algorithm giving more than 1.8n points for arbitrarily large n. The MCTS result covers 82 to 119 only and does not meet that stated target. Searches found no event in 2024 on this problem. Neighbouring 2026 work (the k ≥ 3 no-(k+1)-in-line result, checkerboard variants, infinite sets, the three-dimensional problem) is recorded with reasons and excluded.
competing_reading: Read the 2026 batch as substantive progress. f(n) = 2n is now settled for every n ≤ 76 except 75, up from n ≤ 46 at the start of 2024, and the planar constant has a worked-out heuristic that Kudriashov reproduces and that the field now cites. The opposite reading: each settled n is one more instance of a question whose content is asymptotic, the asymptotic conjecture is untouched, the 1.8n result is empirical, and the constant is a heuristic correction from 2004 that the 2026 papers reproduce rather than prove. On AI, a reader could say Kudriashov's disclosure makes AI load-bearing for the planar material, and that the MCTS paper's 1.8n configurations are AI-found. The opposite reading: the Kudriashov statement covers the whole article's machinery, its planar output is a heuristic constant and not a value of f(n), and the MCTS method is classical search with no learned component.
what_would_settle_it: For the 2n frontier: a Heule write-up or preprint with the SAT encodings or certificates for n = 65–76; a preprint or note for Prellberg's n = 61–68 and 74; a script run over Flammenkamp's database entries for these n (a collinearity check). For the AI questions: Davies's own account of the ChatGPT 5.6 Sol work; the PDF of arXiv 2609.25133, Section 9 and Part III, to check the quoted sentences here; and which n the 17 August rot2 solutions come from in that paper. For the 1.8n result: the per-n sizes and the fit method (Table 1, Figure 6a, Appendix F), and any independent check of the configurations. For the constant: a referee report or journal acceptance for Prellberg's and Kudriashov's heuristic derivations, or a proof that the residual error is O(n) rather than Θ(n ln n).
